title: 2-D DP: Longest Common Subsequence
oneLiner: The longest sequence of characters that appears in both strings in the same order (not necessarily adjacent) -- filled cell by cell in a prefix-by-prefix table.
keyTakeaway: dp[i][j] = the LCS length of a's first i characters and b's first j. If a[i-1] == b[j-1], that character extends the diagonal: dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. Otherwise drop the last character of one string or the other: max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Row 0 and column 0 are all 0.
explanation:
A subsequence keeps some characters of a string in their original order and deletes the rest: "ace" is a subsequence of "abcde", "aec" is not. Given two strings, return the length of the longest subsequence they share. For "abcde" and "ace" it's 3 ("ace" itself). This is the core of diff tools: the lines two files have in common, in order, are their LCS, and everything else is an insertion or a deletion.

Brute force would list all 2^n subsequences of one string. Instead, ask about prefixes and look only at their last characters. Let dp[i][j] be the LCS length of a's first i characters and b's first j. If a[i-1] == b[j-1], some longest common subsequence ends with that shared character, so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. If they differ, at least one of the two last characters isn't in the LCS, so throw one away and keep the better result: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). An empty prefix shares nothing, so row 0 and column 0 are 0.

Fill the (len(a)+1) × (len(b)+1) table row by row, left to right; each cell needs only the cell above, the cell to the left and the one up-left, which are already filled. The answer is the bottom-right cell. That is O(n · m) time and space, and since a row only needs the row above it, two rows (O(m) space) are enough when you only need the length.

Interviewers usually follow up by asking for the subsequence itself: keep the full table and walk back from the bottom-right corner, moving diagonally (and collecting the character) when the characters match, otherwise moving toward whichever neighbour, up or left, holds the larger value. The visualization's last step highlights that path. Related problems with the same table: the minimum deletions to make two strings equal (len(a) + len(b) - 2 × LCS), the shortest common supersequence (len(a) + len(b) - LCS), and longest palindromic subsequence (LCS of a string and its reverse).

visualizationSteps.message: Rows are prefixes of "abcde", columns are prefixes of "ace" ("-" is the empty prefix). Row 0 and column 0 are 0: an empty string shares nothing.
Row 1 ('a'): it matches 'a' at column 1, so that cell (bright) is the up-left diagonal (green) + 1 = 1. Every other cell takes max(up, left).
Row 2 ('b'): 'b' appears nowhere in "ace", so every cell just copies max(up, left) -- this row equals the row above.
Row 3 ('c'): it matches 'c' at column 2, so that cell (bright) is the up-left diagonal (green) + 1 = 2. Every other cell takes max(up, left).
Row 4 ('d'): 'd' appears nowhere in "ace", so every cell just copies max(up, left) -- this row equals the row above.
Row 5 ('e'): it matches 'e' at column 3, so that cell (bright) is the up-left diagonal (green) + 1 = 3. Every other cell takes max(up, left).

The answer is the bottom-right cell: 3. To recover the subsequence, walk back from there: on a match step diagonally and keep the character (bright), otherwise step toward the larger of up and left. Reading the kept characters backwards gives "ace".

recognitionSignals: Two strings or sequences and "longest" something they share in order, where gaps are allowed (common subsequence, matching lines in a diff).
The answer for two whole strings depends on the answer for their prefixes after dropping a last character from one or both.
Problems phrased as "minimum deletions to make them equal" or "shortest string containing both" that reduce to LCS arithmetic.
gotchas: A subsequence is not a substring. For longest common SUBSTRING, a mismatch resets the cell to 0 instead of taking max(up, left).
The table has an extra row and column for the empty prefix, so cell (i, j) compares a[i-1] with b[j-1]. Off-by-one here is the most common bug.
On a match, use the DIAGONAL plus 1, not max(up, left) plus 1 -- the latter can count the same character twice.
confusableWith: 2-D DP: Edit Distance (this track) uses the same two-prefix table and fills it in the same order, but it MINIMIZES edits (1 + min of three neighbours on a mismatch) while LCS MAXIMIZES shared characters (max of two neighbours).
Dynamic Programming: Longest Increasing Subsequence (Fundamentals) is also a "longest subsequence" problem, but over ONE sequence with a 1-D table.

complexity.note: One O(1) cell per pair of prefixes: (n+1) × (m+1) cells. Keeping only the previous row cuts space to O(m).
